 NOVEMBER, DOOR BY DOOR
 October 30, 2026 
 by FOLIO 
 16 mins read 
 Thirty days, one long walk around the world, and a welcome waiting at every stop. 
 By Neha Nidheesh 
 November has a way of making the world look familiar. The weather changes, the holidays approach, and the year begins its slow countdown to December. But while some of us are planning Thanksgiving dinners or reaching for our winter clothes, the rest of the world is busy doing things we might never imagine. 
 Rivers become stages for glowing celebrations. Streets come alive with music, colour and centuries-old traditions. Families gather to honour their ancestors, celebrate new beginnings or keep stories alive that have travelled through generations. 
 November isn’t just a month on the calendar. It’s a window into how differently people celebrate life, remember their past and come together. 
 And some of the most fascinating celebrations happen far beyond the traditions we already know. 
 NOV. 1–2 | MEXICO 
 Día de los Muertos: A place for those we carry with us 
 For Día de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, many Mexican families prepare a welcome for loved ones who have died. The preparations might begin with a photograph taken from a drawer, a favourite recipe brought out again or flowers chosen for a place of remembrance. 
 At home, families may create an ofrenda, an altar arranged with photographs, candles, flowers, food and treasured belongings. Orange marigolds, known as cempasúchil, are closely associated with the occasion. Bakeries prepare pan de muerto, a special bread made for the season, while families may include the foods and personal objects that remind them of those they miss. 
 The observance brings together Indigenous traditions and Catholic influences, with customs that differ across regions and families. No two altars need to look alike. One might hold a grandfather’s favourite sweet, another a child’s toy, and another a photograph beside a cup of coffee prepared just as someone once liked it. 
 UNESCO inscribed the Indigenous festivity dedicated to the dead in Mexico on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008. Its significance lies in the knowledge, rituals and family traditions that continue to be passed down, not simply in the colourful displays for which the occasion is known. 
 Children may learn about relatives they never had the chance to meet. An aunt’s story is told again. A familiar dish brings back a grandmother’s kitchen. Someone remembers a laugh so clearly that the whole family begins laughing, too. 
 The people being remembered are not reduced to photographs or stories. They remain part of the family’s understanding of itself through the habits, recipes, memories and affection that continue across generations. 
 There is no single way to remember someone. For many Mexican families, these days offer a special opportunity to do so together. 
 NOV. 1–2 | BOLIVIA 
 Todos Santos and Día de los Difuntos: The table is ready 
 As November begins, many Bolivian households prepare for Todos Santos and Día de los Difuntos, observances that honour the departed through traditions shaped by Andean beliefs and Catholic practice. 
 In some communities, families arrange a mesa, a table with flowers, candles, photographs, drinks, favourite foods and special breads. Among the best known are t’antawawas, breads shaped like small human figures. Other breads may represent ladders or horses, although their forms and meanings vary by region. 
 For many families, Nov. 1 is associated with welcoming the souls of loved ones, while Nov. 2 brings visits to cemeteries and prayers for the departed. The ways these days are observed differ across communities, and families may follow their own customs. 
 The preparations can take hours. Bread is made, flowers are arranged, and each item is placed with care. Older relatives explain the significance of the food and symbols to younger family members, who learn the tradition by helping to prepare it. 
 In some places, families share food with people who stop to pray at the table or cemetery. Such gestures reflect the hospitality associated with certain local observances, although they are not universal. 
 What stands out is the care given to remembering. A table is not prepared in a hurry. The person being honoured has a history, a place in the family and details worth recalling. Someone remembers what they liked to eat; someone else remembers a story that has not been told for a while. 
 Here, remembrance is expressed through the work of preparing, the act of gathering and the stories that are told along the way. 
 NOV. 3 | AUSTRALIA 
 Melbourne Cup Day: A race brings people together 
 On the first Tuesday of November, attention turns to Flemington Racecourse in Melbourne for the Melbourne Cup, one of Australia’s best-known horse races. 
 First run in 1861, the Cup covers 3,200 metres and has become a major event in Australia’s sporting and social calendar. Melbourne Cup Day is a public holiday across Victoria, although some non-metropolitan councils arrange an alternative local holiday. 
 For some, the day is about following the racing. For others, it is an occasion to dress up, share lunch with colleagues or gather with friends. Even people who rarely follow horse racing may find themselves drawn into a conversation about which horse someone has chosen. 
 The Cup also brings serious discussion about horse welfare and the responsibilities of the racing industry. Those concerns are an important part of the event’s contemporary story and deserve consideration alongside its sporting history. 
 Not everyone celebrates the day, and its significance varies across the country. Yet the event remains a familiar fixture in Australia’s November calendar, bringing people together in settings that range from the racecourse to the workplace. 
 There is something recognisable about the anticipation surrounding a shared event. People make predictions, exchange opinions and watch the same few minutes unfold. For some, the memory that lasts is the race itself. For others, it is the people they spent the afternoon with. 
 NOV. 5 | LIBERIA 
 National Thanksgiving Day: A day for gratitude 
 Liberia observes National Thanksgiving Day on the first Thursday of November. In 2026, it falls on Nov. 5. Established by legislation in 1883, the observance is associated with prayer, worship and reflection. 
 Families and religious communities mark the day in different ways. Some attend services, while others spend time with relatives or gather for a meal. For many, it is an opportunity to give thanks for life, faith, family and the support of their community. 
 Liberia’s history includes the arrival of settlers from the United States in the 19th century, as well as the much longer histories of the Indigenous peoples whose lives and cultures are rooted in the land. The country’s story encompasses different experiences of belonging, identity and faith. Its Thanksgiving observance is part of that history, though no single day can represent the beliefs or experiences of every Liberian. 
 Gratitude does not always require a grand occasion. It can be a prayer for someone who has been unwell, a visit to a relative or a quiet recognition of the people who offered help when it was needed. 
 A national day of thanksgiving gives people time to pause and reflect on what sustains them. The meaning may be personal, shared with a family or expressed through a place of worship. 
 NOV. 5 | UNITED KINGDOM 
 Bonfire Night: An evening beneath a bright sky 
 On the same date, communities across parts of the United Kingdom gather for Bonfire Night, also known as Guy Fawkes Night. 
 The occasion recalls the Gunpowder Plot of 1605, a failed conspiracy to destroy the Houses of Parliament and kill King James I. Guy Fawkes was discovered guarding explosives beneath the building, and his name became closely associated with the event. 
 The plot unfolded during a period of religious tension and discrimination against Catholics. Parliament established a day of thanksgiving for the plot’s failure in 1606. The Nov. 5 observance continued long after the original legislation was repealed in 1859. 
 Today, many people mark the evening with organised fireworks displays, bonfires and community gatherings. Children watch the sky, friends meet outdoors, and warm drinks help take the edge off the November air. 
 People relate to the history in different ways, and not everyone celebrates. For those who attend a local display, however, the evening may be a familiar part of the season. Neighbours stand together in coats and scarves, faces turned upwards as fireworks briefly light the sky. 
 A public celebration can create a meeting place for people who might otherwise pass one another without speaking. For an evening, they share the same patch of ground and the same view. 
 NOV. 8 | INDIA 
 Diwali: A festival of light and homecoming 
 In India, the days around Diwali bring preparations that often begin well before the first lamps are lit. Homes are cleaned, sweets are made, flowers are chosen, and doorways may be decorated with rangoli, patterns created with coloured powders, rice flour or flower petals. 
 In 2026, the main day of Diwali falls on Sunday, Nov. 8, in India. The wider festival period includes other observances, though dates and customs vary by region and religious calendar. 
 Diwali, also known as Deepavali, is celebrated by many Hindus, Jains and Sikhs, with distinct meanings within each tradition. Many Hindu families associate the festival with Rama’s return to Ayodhya or worship Lakshmi, who is associated with prosperity and good fortune. Jain communities connect the occasion with Mahavira’s attainment of liberation. Sikhs observe Bandi Chhor Divas, remembering Guru Hargobind’s release from imprisonment alongside other prisoners. Its date often coincides with Diwali, but it has its own history and significance. 
 The celebrations differ from home to home. Clay lamps called diyas may be placed along windowsills and doorways. Families offer prayers, exchange sweets and visit relatives. In some households, preparations fill the day; in others, the celebration is quieter. 
 Often, it is the smallest details that stay with people. A child carefully placing a lamp where a parent has shown them. A plate of sweets carried to a neighbour. A recipe that appears once a year and tastes exactly as it did in childhood. 
 For families living far from relatives, the occasion can be a chance to reconnect. For others, it is a time for prayer, reflection or welcoming a fresh beginning. There is no single experience that captures every family’s Diwali. 
 As the lamps begin to glow, familiar rooms take on a different appearance. Light gathers around doorways and courtyards, and the people who have spent the day preparing can finally sit together. The festival’s meaning is carried not only by the lights themselves, but by the faith, memories and relationships that give them a place in the home. 
 NOV. 8 | UNITED KINGDOM 
 Remembrance Sunday: Two minutes to remember 
 On the second Sunday of November, Remembrance Sunday is observed across the United Kingdom. In 2026, it falls on Nov. 8. At war memorials throughout the country, people gather to honour those who served and those who died in the two world wars and later conflicts. 
 The national service takes place at the Cenotaph on Whitehall in London. At 11 a.m., a two-minute silence is observed, and red poppies are widely worn as a symbol of remembrance. 
 For some families, the day brings a particular person to mind: a relative whose story was passed down, a photograph kept for decades or a life changed by war. Others gather to remember people they never knew but whose experiences shaped the world they inherited. 
 Remembrance Sunday is distinct from Armistice Day on Nov. 11, which marks the 1918 armistice that ended fighting on the Western Front in the First World War. A further silence is observed at 11 a.m. on Armistice Day. 
 The ceremonies are public, but remembrance is often deeply personal. A name on a memorial may mean little to a passerby and everything to a family. A poppy may represent a personal memory, an act of respect or a connection to someone else’s story. 
 For two minutes, people set aside their conversations and daily tasks. The silence does not make the history of war simple, but it gives people a moment to recognise the lives behind it. 
 NOV. 9 | FIJI 
 Diwali: A light carried across generations 
 In Fiji, Diwali is a public holiday observed on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, following the festival on Sunday, Nov. 8. 
 The celebration has a particular place in the lives of many Indo-Fijian families. Its history in Fiji is connected with the arrival of Indian indentured labourers under British colonial rule. The first ship carrying indentured workers, the Leonidas, arrived in 1879. Over the following decades, tens of thousands of people travelled from India under labour agreements known as girmit. The term girmitiya is associated with those who lived through the system and their descendants. 
 The history of indenture includes hardship and unequal conditions. It is also part of the story of families and communities that grew across generations. Indo-Fijian communities have contributed to Fiji’s cultural life, including its food, languages, music and religious traditions. 
 For many families celebrating Diwali, the familiar preparations include lights, prayers, sweets and visits with loved ones. The details vary, and each household has its own ways of marking the occasion. 
 A tradition can travel with people and take root in a new place. A recipe is passed down, a prayer is taught to a child, and a familiar celebration becomes part of the home the next generation knows. The landscape may be different from the one remembered by a grandparent, but the act of gathering can still carry a sense of continuity. 
 In Fiji, Diwali is part of a living cultural story, shaped by the people who observe it and the communities among whom they live. 
 AROUND NOV. 15 | JAPAN 
 Shichi-Go-San: The years that seem to pass overnight 
 In Japan, Shichi-Go-San is a traditional celebration honouring children at the ages of three, five and seven. Its name means “seven-five-three,” referring to the ages marked by the occasion. 
 Families often visit Shinto shrines to give thanks for their children’s growth and pray for their continued health and wellbeing. Children may wear formal clothing, including kimono, and families often take photographs to remember the day. Although Nov. 15 is the traditional date, many families arrange visits on nearby days that fit their schedules. 
 One of the best-known treats associated with the celebration is chitose ame, or “thousand-year candy.” The long, thin sweets are traditionally linked with wishes for a long and healthy life. They are often presented in decorated bags featuring auspicious symbols such as cranes and turtles. 
 The observance is a chance to recognise how much a child has grown. A little one who once needed help with every step may now walk into the shrine holding a parent’s hand. A child who once hid behind a familiar face may stand proudly for a photograph. 
 Families celebrate in different ways, but the wishes at the heart of the occasion are familiar: health, happiness and many years ahead. 
 Years later, those photographs may be brought out again. The clothes will look small, the expressions will seem wonderfully serious, and someone will remember the effort it took to get everyone ready. 
 Shichi-Go-San marks a moment in childhood, but it also holds a place for the family members who have watched over that child. The photographs help preserve one particular stage of a life that is still unfolding. 
 NOV. 20 | BRAZIL 
 Dia Nacional de Zumbi e da Consciência Negra: Remembering a history that continues to shape the present 
 Brazil observes Nov. 20 as the Dia Nacional de Zumbi e da Consciência Negra, or National Day of Zumbi and Black Consciousness. The date honours Zumbi dos Palmares, a leader remembered for resisting slavery. 
 Zumbi was associated with Palmares, a network of communities known as quilombos. These communities were formed by people who escaped enslavement, alongside others, and became important places of community life and resistance. Palmares was located in what is now the state of Alagoas, and Zumbi died on Nov. 20, 1695. 
 The date is an opportunity to recognise the history and contributions of Black Brazilians. Their influence can be found throughout Brazil’s music, literature, food, faith, art and public life. It is also a time to reflect on the continuing effects of slavery and racism. 
 Brazil formally abolished slavery in 1888. In December 2023, federal law established Nov. 20 as a national public holiday, first observed under that law in 2024. 
 Events may include performances, educational programmes, discussions and community gatherings. The ways people mark the day differ, but its place in the national calendar recognises histories and achievements that deserve attention throughout the year. 
 To remember Zumbi and Palmares is to remember people who sought freedom and built communities under difficult circumstances. It is also to recognise the Black Brazilians who continue to shape the country’s future. 
 A country’s history becomes more complete when more of its people are heard. The stories passed down through families, the culture created by artists and communities, and the work of those building a more equal future all belong to that history. 
 NOV. 24 | THAILAND 
 Loy Krathong: A little boat on the water 
 On the evening of Loy Krathong, people across Thailand gather beside rivers, canals, ponds and lakes with small decorated floats called krathong. 
 The word loy means to float. A traditional krathong may be made from banana leaves and other natural materials, with flowers, a candle and incense arranged on top. The festival follows the full moon of the 12th month in the traditional Thai lunar calendar. In 2026, Loy Krathong is expected to fall on Nov. 24. 
 The meanings associated with Loy Krathong differ across communities. Some people express gratitude to water, while others make wishes, offer prayers or use the moment to symbolically let go of worries. 
 Preparing a krathong can be a careful process. Leaves are folded, flowers are arranged, and a candle is placed in the centre. As evening falls, families and friends make their way to the water and set their floats adrift. 
 In northern Thailand, Yi Peng takes place around the same period and belongs to the region’s Lanna cultural traditions. It is associated with lantern displays. The two observances may coincide, but they are distinct traditions with their own histories and meanings. 
 Communities increasingly encourage biodegradable materials and responsible clean-up to protect waterways after the festivities. It is a practical consideration that sits naturally beside the celebration’s connection with water. 
 A river may be part of everyday life, carrying boats, reflecting the sky and sustaining the communities beside it. On Loy Krathong, people pause to acknowledge that relationship. A little float carries a wish into the night, and the water remains part of the story long after the candle disappears from view. 
 NOV. 26 | UNITED STATES 
 Thanksgiving: A place at the table 
 Thanksgiving falls on the fourth Thursday of November. In 2026, it arrives on Nov. 26. 
 For many Americans, the day begins with familiar preparations. A family recipe is brought out, someone asks what they should bring, and chairs are arranged for relatives travelling from near and far. Others share a meal with friends, volunteer to serve food or spend the day quietly. 
 The holiday is often linked to a harvest gathering at Plymouth in 1621 involving English colonists and Wampanoag people. That gathering was one event in a much longer history. Indigenous nations had their own traditions of giving thanks long before the arrival of European settlers, and colonisation brought profound changes, dispossession and loss to Native communities. 
 In 1863, during the Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln proclaimed a national day of thanksgiving for the last Thursday of November. The federal holiday is now observed on the fourth Thursday. 
 People mark Thanksgiving in many ways. For some, it is a treasured family gathering. For others, it means sharing food with friends, helping a community organisation or calling someone who cannot be there in person. Native American experiences and perspectives also differ. Since 1970, the United American Indians of New England have gathered in Plymouth on Thanksgiving for the National Day of Mourning, drawing attention to Indigenous histories and continuing concerns. 
 A respectful account of Thanksgiving has room for gratitude and for an honest understanding of the past. The two can exist together. 
 At a table, people may bring different memories and different understandings of the day. Listening to those stories can make a gathering more meaningful. The food may be familiar, but the people around it each carry a history of their own. 
 NOV. 30 | SCOTLAND 
 St Andrew’s Day: A song before the month ends 
 November closes in Scotland with St Andrew’s Day, a celebration associated with the country’s patron saint and Scottish culture. 
 St Andrew has long been revered in Scotland, and the saltire, the white diagonal cross on a blue field, is associated with him. St Andrew’s Day became the subject of a statutory bank holiday under legislation passed in 2007, although whether workplaces close depends on local arrangements and employers. 
 The day may be marked with traditional food, music, cultural events and gatherings. A ceilidh, a social gathering often involving traditional music and dancing, can bring people onto the floor while a caller helps everyone follow the steps. Families may share a meal, visit heritage sites or join community celebrations. Scottish communities abroad mark the occasion, too. 
 There is no single way to express Scottish identity. For some, it is tied to a town, a family history or a language. For others, it lives in a song learned in childhood, a dish prepared for a special occasion or a story shared by an older relative. 
 Traditions are kept alive by people who continue to make room for them. A song is taught to a child, a recipe is passed along, and a dance brings strangers into the same circle. Each generation inherits something, then adds its own memories. 
 By the last day of November, the year is beginning to look towards December. But there is still time for one more gathering, one more tune and one more meal shared among people who have made the journey to be together. 
 ALL MONTH | ANTARCTICA 
 Life on the ice: A different kind of November 
 Antarctica offers a different story. It has no permanent civilian population or Indigenous communities with a shared traditional November holiday calendar, and there is no continent-wide November festival comparable to those observed elsewhere. 
 November falls within the Austral spring. Daylight is increasing, and research activity grows at stations across the continent. Scientists and support teams prepare for fieldwork shaped by the weather, the landscape and the needs of each research programme. Depending on the location, they may study ice, oceans, wildlife, atmospheric conditions or wider environmental change. 
 People living temporarily at research stations may mark birthdays, national holidays or personal milestones together. These are individual or station-based occasions rather than a single Antarctic tradition shared by everyone. 
 Far from home, a small celebration can be meaningful. A cake prepared with the supplies available, a favourite song played in a shared room or a message from family can bring a familiar feeling into an unfamiliar place. 
 The Antarctic Treaty, signed in 1959 and in force since 1961, provides a framework for peaceful use and international scientific cooperation on the continent. Research there depends on the efforts of people from many countries, working in demanding conditions to understand a place that affects the wider planet. 
 Antarctica reminds us that not every November story begins with a festival. Sometimes it is about the people working together, looking after one another and sharing the discoveries that come from patient observation. 
 A WORLD OF TRADITIONS, A SHARED HUMANITY 
 Across the world, November brings moments that mean something special to someone. A photograph is placed beside a candle. A lamp is lit at home. A family gathers in prayer. A nation pauses to remember. A community honours the people and stories that helped shape its history. 
 The traditions may be different, but each holds something precious: a memory, a belief, a story or a connection passed from one generation to the next. 
 We may not know every tradition, but we can always make room to learn about it. And sometimes, the world feels a little closer simply because we took the time to understand. 
 Different places. Different stories. So much to discover.
